paragraphs.heading: Three rock types, one loop
paragraphs.text: The rock cycle is a basic idea in geology. It describes how the three main rock types, sedimentary, metamorphic and igneous, change into one another through geologic time. Whatever its type, a rock is altered when something forces it out of its equilibrium conditions. Plate tectonics and the water cycle are the driving forces, so rocks do not stay in equilibrium and change as they meet new environments.

paragraphs.heading: Breaking down into sediment
paragraphs.text: Rocks exposed to the atmosphere are unstable to varying degrees. Weathering and erosion break them into smaller fragments and carry away dissolved material. The fragments pile up, are buried by more material and are compacted. Sedimentary rock can form by lithification of these buried fragments, of material made by living organisms, or of material that came out of a mineral-bearing solution through evaporation.

paragraphs.heading: Changed by heat and pressure
paragraphs.text: High temperatures and pressures can change a rock physically or chemically and make it a metamorphic rock. The process is called metamorphism, and it can modify any rock that already exists. Regional metamorphism affects large masses of rock over a wide area and is typically tied to mountain building. Contact metamorphism happens when a body of rock touches an igneous intrusion that heats it.

paragraphs.heading: Melting and cooling
paragraphs.text: Rocks pushed deep below the surface melt into magma. When conditions no longer keep the magma liquid, it cools and crystallizes into an igneous rock. Any of the three rock types can take this path. Rock that cools inside the Earth cools very slowly and has a coarse-grained texture, as in granite. Magma that reaches the surface is called lava and may cool very rapidly, giving fine-grained rocks and sometimes a natural glass such as obsidian.

paragraphs.heading: Plate tectonics as the engine
paragraphs.text: Plate tectonics came to be recognized as the driving force for the rock cycle. At mid-ocean ridges, where plates move apart, new magma is produced and the new rock is carried away from the ridge. This new basaltic ocean crust eventually meets a subduction zone and is pulled back into the mantle. Rising pressure and temperature there rearrange its minerals, and this metamorphism turns the rock into eclogite.

paragraphs.heading: Back to magma
paragraphs.text: As the slab of crust is dragged deeper, water and other volatile materials are driven off and rise into the wedge of rock above the subduction zone. The material in this wedge melts. The buoyant magma rises through the rock above and produces volcanism in island arcs or at continental margins. So a single igneous rock such as basalt has more than one possible fate: exposed to the atmosphere it may break down and dissolve, or it may melt while being subducted under a continent.
